items.readable_text:
Content:
When rounding whole numbers to the nearest ten, we sometimes need to adjust the hundreds, tens, and ones.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's round the following number to the nearest ten:

Content:
[MATH: 298]

Content:
As usual, we start by writing our number into a place value chart, highlighting the tens place:

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 9] | [MATH: 8] |

Content:
We then look one digit to the right in the chart (this will be the ones place) and compare it to the number [MATH: 5{:}]

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 9] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}8}] |

Content:
Since [MATH: \color{red}8] is greater or equal to [MATH: 5], we must round up. To do this, we follow the usual algorithm:

Content:
- We put [MATH: \color{blue}0] in the ones place and increase the tens value by one:

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 9\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}+1}] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] |

Content:
- However, [MATH: 9+1=10] tens is the same as [MATH: 1] hundred and [MATH: 0] tens. So, we must write [MATH: 0] in the tens place and increase the number of hundreds by one:

Content:
| hundreds | tens | ones |
| [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3}] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}] | [MATH: 0] |

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 298] rounded to the nearest ten is [MATH: 300.]
